text.text: I’m a software developer and problem solver. I like getting close enough to a complicated problem to make it workable.
My professional grounding is in Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations and ERP. That means thinking about software alongside the people, processes and information it has to support.

I work through requirements, technical design, implementation, testing, deployment and support. Cross-team coordination matters throughout: a solution has to make sense to the people requesting it, building it and living with it.
I’m interested in the whole path from “what do we actually need?” to “does this still work when someone uses it?” The handoffs are part of the work, not an afterthought.

This small workspace is a way to share how I think. There isn’t a catalogue of client work or a set of performance claims here. You can read about my approach, look through my interests, or get in touch directly.
Start with Approach for the working process, or Curiosity for the things I keep exploring outside it.
I think of delivery as one connected piece of work. Writing the code is important; understanding what comes before and after is just as important.

Start with the person and the process. Clarify what needs to change, what already works, and what constraints the solution has to respect. In ERP work, a technical choice can affect a business workflow far beyond one screen.

Translate requirements into a technical design that people can discuss. Surface dependencies, integration points and tradeoffs early. Keep the problem visible so that the implementation doesn’t become an answer to a different question.

Implementation and testing belong together. Check the expected behavior, the awkward cases and the points where systems or teams meet. A piece of code working by itself is not the same as a usable end-to-end solution.
Deployment, support and coordination complete the loop. Think about how a change reaches users and how problems can be understood afterwards. Feedback from real use is part of improving the solution.

For smaller freelance work, I’m interested in contained needs that fit remote, evening or asynchronous collaboration. Clear boundaries help make useful progress without promising more availability than I have.
These are working principles, not a fabricated project history or a claim about measured client outcomes.
Some of the most interesting learning happens when there isn’t a delivery deadline attached to it.
I’m interested in homelab and server setups, including Raspberry Pi. Small systems are a good reason to think about how software is hosted, connected and maintained—not just how it is written.
There’s something satisfying about following a question all the way through the stack: what runs where, what depends on what, and what happens when something stops working?

I’m curious about AI-assisted work processes and web apps. Where does assistance remove friction? Where is human judgment still the essential step? I’m interested in useful applications, not adding a chatbot to everything.
How can a complicated process become easier to understand without hiding what matters?
What is the simplest setup that is still understandable and maintainable?
How do we check whether assistance actually helps the person doing the work?
An interests notebook, not a list of shipped projects or demonstrated results. The questions are illustrative prompts for exploration.
The direct route is LinkedIn. Tell me what you’re working through and what kind of help you’re looking for.
I’m open to discussing contained freelance work that fits remote, evening or asynchronous collaboration. I’m employed full-time, so scope and timing need to be realistic from the start.
I’m interested in senior developer and technical-lead opportunities where end-to-end problem solving and cross-team coordination matter.

I work through requirements, technical design, implementation, testing, deployment and support. Cross-team coordination matters throughout: a solution has to make sense to the people requesting it, building it and living with it.
I’m interested in the whole path from “what do we actually need?” to “does this still work when someone uses it?” The handoffs are part of the work, not an afterthought.

This small workspace is a way to share how I think. There isn’t a catalogue of client work or a set of performance claims here. You can read about my approach, look through my interests, or get in touch directly.
Start with Approach for the working process, or Curiosity for the things I keep exploring outside it.
I think of delivery as one connected piece of work. Writing the code is important; understanding what comes before and after is just as important.

Start with the person and the process. Clarify what needs to change, what already works, and what constraints the solution has to respect. In ERP work, a technical choice can affect a business workflow far beyond one screen.

Translate requirements into a technical design that people can discuss. Surface dependencies, integration points and tradeoffs early. Keep the problem visible so that the implementation doesn’t become an answer to a different question.

Implementation and testing belong together. Check the expected behavior, the awkward cases and the points where systems or teams meet. A piece of code working by itself is not the same as a usable end-to-end solution.
Deployment, support and coordination complete the loop. Think about how a change reaches users and how problems can be understood afterwards. Feedback from real use is part of improving the solution.

For smaller freelance work, I’m interested in contained needs that fit remote, evening or asynchronous collaboration. Clear boundaries help make useful progress without promising more availability than I have.
These are working principles, not a fabricated project history or a claim about measured client outcomes.
Some of the most interesting learning happens when there isn’t a delivery deadline attached to it.
I’m interested in homelab and server setups, including Raspberry Pi. Small systems are a good reason to think about how software is hosted, connected and maintained—not just how it is written.
There’s something satisfying about following a question all the way through the stack: what runs where, what depends on what, and what happens when something stops working?

I’m curious about AI-assisted work processes and web apps. Where does assistance remove friction? Where is human judgment still the essential step? I’m interested in useful applications, not adding a chatbot to everything.
How can a complicated process become easier to understand without hiding what matters?
What is the simplest setup that is still understandable and maintainable?
How do we check whether assistance actually helps the person doing the work?
